newsitem.title: USA: Soymeal exports, margins seen keeping US crush up.
newsitem.headline: Soymeal exports, margins seen keeping US crush up.

text.p: The ongoing brisk pace of soymeal export shipments and strong nearby crush margins should keep the pace of the U.S. soybean crush near record levels in the near term, most analysts and dealers said.

"We've had margin improvement on the (futures) board," said Dave Armstrong, grain analyst with Chicago Corp. brokerage in Chicago. "The best margins you see are nearby, and I don't see any reason that they're (crushers) going to slow down."
On Thursday, the National Oilseed Processors Association reported the weekly soybean crushing pace was much higher than expected at 30.864 million bushels.

Additionally on Thursday, the U.S. Census Bureau reported the monthly crush for December and January was the highest in two years. In December, the crush was 138.218 million bushels, and in January it was 137.265 million, the Bureau reported.
Armstrong said he did not expect the crush to fall below 29 million bushels before the second week of March, when soymeal from South America hits world export markets.
But for the near term, the pace of soymeal export shipments remains strong enough to keep soybean processors crushing, analysts and dealers said.
"As long as you are shipping that aggressively you have to keep making a lot of meal," Armstrong said.
On Friday, the U.S. Department of Agriculture reported that soymeal exports for the week ended February 13 were 179,200 tonnes.
That pace was below last week's pace of 306,400 tonnes, but still strong enough to support the crush, Armstrong said.
However some dealers disagreed and said the dropoff in soymeal export shipments this week was a sign that the market is softening. They predicted the crushing pace will ease next week as a result.
"It's going to slow up all of a sudden," said one soymeal broker in Tennessee. "The demand valves will start to shut off, and then you'll see the crush go down."

One soymeal dealer in the truck market said he expected the pace of the crush to continue at very high levels in the near term unless news that China cancelled large amounts of soymeal business proved to be true.
"I haven't seen any indication in my area that the crush is going to slow down at all," the dealer said. "I do think things will slow if the Chinese really cancelled that much business."

The cash and futures markets were rife with rumors Friday that China canceled as much as 450,000 tonnes of soymeal export business from South America and India. No confirmation of the dealings could be immediately obtained, however.
